https://www.foxnews.com/world/nato-membe.text: Poland, the closest NATO member to the Ukraine-Russia war, scrambled fighter jets and placed its air defenses on high alert early Thursday as Russia launched more than 70 missiles and roughly 280 drones across Ukraine, killing at least eight and wounding dozens from Kyiv to the western city of Lviv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, just returning from this week's U.S. visit with President Donald Trump and the funeral of late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., said the barrage exposed a critical shortage of Western-supplied interceptors, particularly against ballistic missiles. "The protection of people’s lives depends directly on their willingness" to provide Ukraine with air-defense missiles, Zelenskyy said of Kyiv’s allies. Hours later Thursday morning, the European Union disbursed $4 billion to Ukraine to finance the procurement of more drones, missiles, air defense and fighter jets, according to the European Commission. RUSSIA LAUNCHES BALLISTIC MISSILE ATTACK ON KYIV HOURS AFTER ZELENSKYY WARNS OF MAJOR STRIKE The disbursement is part of a more than $100 billion loan approved by the EU earlier this year and follows the roughly $3.5 billion installment on June 25 and $4.5 billion on June 30. Polish forces detected an unidentified object moving west through the country’s airspace shortly before 4 a.m. An F-16 was dispatched to intercept it, but the object disappeared from radar minutes later. Authorities subsequently found a crater about 33 feet wide and scattered debris in farmland near Tarnawa-Kolonia, about 1.2 miles from the closest buildings. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said initial evidence indicated the object was a Russian Kh-101 missile, although investigators were still working to confirm its type and origin. THE TWO MOST IMPORTANT AMERICAN WEAPONS SYSTEMS NATO IS EAGER TO HAVE "All the indications are that it was a Russian Kh-101," Tusk said, adding that Polish forces were prepared to shoot it down if it had continued flying toward a populated area. He added the U.S. is interested in joining the investigation, which has initially determined the missile was not intended for Poland territory. The fate of the Ukraine-Russian war might be decided within the next 100 days, Tusk told reporters. The threat to a NATO ally is a new frontier in the long-running war and comes after Zelenskyy pressed senators to advance Graham's sweeping sanctions package. Also, Trump and Zelenskyy discussed U.S. licenses allowing Ukraine to produce Patriot interceptors, along with other defense cooperation and efforts to revive stalled diplomacy with Moscow. Six people, including two girls ages 5 and 12, were killed when a Russian Iskander-M ballistic missile struck a private home housing a large family near Kryvyi Rih, according to local officials. Seven others were reported killed in Kyiv and elsewhere in the Dnipropetrovsk and Poltava regions as the casualty count rose during rescue operations. 'WRITTEN IN OUR DNA': POLISH PILOTS WHO REMEMBER SOVIET RULE PREPARE FOR AMERICA'S MOST LETHAL FIGHTER JET "A dark night," Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of Kryvyi Rih’s defense council, wrote on Telegram. Eight people were wounded in the strike on the home. The person killed in Kyiv was a 31-year-old man, while two others were wounded, according to Ukrainian police. Russian strikes damaged residential buildings, vehicles, storage facilities, a market and a garage complex in the capital, where air raid warnings lasted more than five hours and thousands of residents sheltered in subway stations. In Lviv, about 40 miles from the Polish border, emergency crews searched damaged apartment buildings for people trapped beneath concrete and debris. Thirty people, including children, were reported injured. More than 20 residential buildings, a school and two kindergartens were damaged, officials said. "I was terrified watching the rescuers go beneath those concrete slabs," one Lviv resident told Reuters as crews pulled a boy from a damaged building. Ukraine’s air force said its defenses intercepted 55 missiles and 265 drones. But only one of nine ballistic missiles was shot down, while 11 missiles and 17 drones struck targets at 20 locations. The U.S.-made Patriot is the only system currently in Ukraine’s arsenal capable of reliably intercepting Russian ballistic missiles, which travel at several times the speed of sound. Zelenskyy has repeatedly warned that Patriot interceptors are arriving too slowly and in insufficient numbers. During his Tuesday meeting with Trump, Zelenskyy said the leaders discussed licenses for Patriot interceptor production in Ukraine. He also met with Lockheed Martin executives and told senators that domestic production would be a long-term solution but would not address Ukraine’s immediate shortage of missiles. European countries have offered to pay for additional U.S.-made interceptors. Zelenskyy’s Washington visit coincided with Senate consideration of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, named for the longtime defense hawk and outspoken Ukraine supporter who died unexpectedly earlier this month. The Senate voted 86-12 Tuesday to clear an initial procedural hurdle and voted 84-12 Wednesday to formally proceed with the legislation. Additional votes were still required before final passage. The package would impose sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions, energy projects and vessels accused of helping Moscow evade existing restrictions. It would also authorize tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the five largest purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas and the leading countries facilitating sanctions evasion. The legislation also includes an extension of sanctions targeting Iran’s energy and weapons sectors, a provision sought by the Trump administration. Zelenskyy met with a bipartisan group of senators before the procedural votes and called the legislation an important signal to Russia, Europe and the Ukrainian people. He watched the Senate vote from the chamber’s gallery after attending Graham’s funeral at Washington National Cathedral. Reuters and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

The student-backed list includes professors, teachers, experts, former athletes and other lesser-known candidates. Vučić has said he will step down as president and seek the premiership if his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) wins. He announced on 8 September that parliament would be dissolved and snap elections held on 25 October, saying he would resign on 27 September to lead the SNS campaign. The ruling party has nominated him as its prime ministerial candidate and placed him at the top of the “Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia” list. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/26/at-l.text: At least 11 people were killed and around 30 others were injured following a suicide bomb attack in northwestern Pakistan on Saturday, according to police and rescue officials.The bomber is said to have detonated a vehicle laden with explosives at a roadside police checkpoint.Bilal Faizi, a spokesperson for the provincial emergency service, said the attack had taken place in the district of Dera Ismail Khan in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.The Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) group, or Pakistani Taliban, has claimed responsibility for the bombing.Pakistan has seen increasing militant attacks in recent years, with the TTP claiming many of them.The Counter Extremism Project (CEP) describes the TTP as a "conglomerate" of roughly 40 tribal and non-tribal militant groups primarily fighting against the Pakistani state. The group, founded in late 2007, is allied with the Afghan Taliban, which returned to power in 2021 after overthrowing the US-backed government in Kabul.According to the CEP, TTP militants regularly carry out attacks against security forces, civilians, and political figures across both Pakistan and Afghanistan.This is a developing story. Moneycontrol World Desk October 10, 2026 / 16:17 IST Ireland’s proposal would reduce the European Union’s planned 2028–2034 budget to €1.62 trillion, but countries seeking deeper spending cuts may oppose the compromise, while farmers have criticised the proposed funding levels. Ireland proposes €141B EU budget cut to €1.62 trillion. International aid faces steepest cuts while farm funds stay. Germany wants deeper cuts; EU leaders to discuss next week. Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Register for FREE Webinar Register for FREE Ireland has proposed cutting €141 billion from the European Union’s next seven-year budget in an attempt to bridge divisions among member states over the bloc’s spending priorities. The revised proposal, presented by Ireland as the holder of the EU’s rotating presidency, would bring the budget for 2028–2034 to around €1.62 trillion, an 8% reduction from the European Commission’s original proposal of approximately €1.76 trillion at 2025 prices. The draft seeks to reconcile demands from countries led by Germany for substantial spending cuts with calls from other member states to protect funding for agriculture and regional development. EU leaders are expected to discuss the proposal at a summit in Brussels next week as governments work towards an agreement by the end of the year. Where will the EU budget cuts fall? Related Stories France boosts police presence, hoping to prevent repeat of riots France shooting kills 1, injures 4; Mayor calls it ‘racist, probably Islamophobic’ India-EU FTA to be signed by December 2026, rollout expected by March-April 2027: Piyush Goyal Ireland’s draft distributes reductions unevenly across the bloc’s spending priorities, with international aid facing some of the steepest cuts while agriculture and regional development funding remain relatively protected. Under the proposal, funding for international aid and related external spending would be reduced by around 17%. Allocations intended to strengthen the EU’s economic competitiveness would fall by approximately 13%, while the budget for EU administration would be cut by around 12%. By contrast, combined funding for agriculture and regional development would be reduced by around 3%, reflecting pressure from member states to preserve traditional EU spending programmes. The draft retains approximately €914 billion for agriculture and regional funding, compared with €946 billion in the European Commission’s original proposal. Despite the reductions, the proposed budget would remain significantly larger than the EU’s current 2021–2027 budget, which is worth around €1.2 trillion. The figures remain subject to negotiations among member states. Germany-led group seeks deeper cuts The proposal comes amid divisions over how much the EU should spend during the next budget cycle. Germany is leading a group of countries, including Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden, that have called for cuts of several hundred billion euros from the Commission’s original proposal. These countries have argued for greater financial restraint as national governments face pressure to control public spending. France, meanwhile, has argued that the EU needs sufficient resources to respond to growing challenges, including strengthening its economy, improving competitiveness and addressing security concerns. French President Emmanuel Macron has called for an ambitious European budget to support the bloc’s priorities, including defence. Another group of 17 countries from southern, central and eastern Europe, known as the Friends of Cohesion, is pushing to protect funding for agriculture and regional development. Ireland’s draft attempts to accommodate these competing demands, but it may not satisfy governments seeking deeper reductions. An EU diplomat quoted in a report by Politico criticised the proposal as insufficient, arguing that the spending level was unaffordable and that the budget failed to prepare the bloc adequately for future challenges. Irish farmers criticise proposed budget The proposed funding levels have drawn criticism from the Irish Farmers’ Association (IFA), which described the draft as a major disappointment for farmers. IFA President Francie Gorman said the Irish proposal had not improved on the European Commission’s earlier plans to cut the budget for the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). According to the IFA, the Commission’s original proposal would have reduced the EU’s CAP budget by 22%, potentially resulting in a 24% reduction in payments to Irish farmers. The association said the proposed allocation of €293 billion for the CAP was insufficient. Gorman argued that €500 billion was needed to strengthen farm resilience, encourage younger people to enter the sector, support food security and improve sustainability. The €500 billion figure is the IFA’s stated funding demand, not an agreed EU allocation. EU leaders face budget deadline Ireland’s draft is intended to provide a basis for further negotiations rather than represent a final settlement. The EU’s 27 leaders will need to reconcile demands for spending restraint with calls for greater investment. The negotiations also involve proposed new EU-wide revenue sources, including levies linked to carbon emissions, carbon-intensive imports, electronic waste, tobacco and large companies. Ireland has retained the proposed measures in its draft, although several have faced opposition from member states. Governments are aiming to reach an agreement by the end of the year. Reports on the negotiations have warned that elections in France, Italy and Poland could complicate efforts to secure a deal if talks are delayed. EU leaders will discuss the Irish proposal at the Brussels summit next week, with the main challenge being to find a compromise acceptable to countries demanding deeper cuts and those seeking to protect funding for agriculture, regional development and other EU priorities.
